articles.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
articles.summary:
Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires

For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.

Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.

articles.title: Nigel Starmer-Smith obituary
articles.summary:
England rugby union player who became one of the best-loved commentators in the game over a 42-year broadcasting career

Nigel Starmer-Smith was an England rugby scrum-half whose international debut at Twickenham, five days before his 25th birthday on Christmas Day in 1969, was a historic first ever win for England over South Africa. But it was as a broadcaster that he was best known. After his playing career ended he became a schoolteacher, then made a move to the BBC where in the 1980s he fronted Rugby Special, a Sunday TV highlights programme, which gave the then-amateur sport of rugby union a wide national audience.

The undisputed voice of rugby was the lilting Scottish brogue of Bill McLaren, but Starmer-Smith, who has died aged 81, became the voice of the English shires. In his clipped, professional tones, he would tell his post-prandial Sunday audience the news from the muddy touchlines of places then familiar on the English rugby map: Bedford, Coventry, Otley, Redruth. Change was in the air, but rugby union was some years from its professional revolution in 1995 and, in England at least, Starmer-Smith represented a now lost cosy world of mud, fellowship and beer.

articles.title: Lloyds emerges as frontrunner to buy Aldermore
articles.summary:
Lloyds has emerged as the frontrunner to buy alternative lender Aldermore after rival bidders dropped out or excluded the group’s motor finance division from their bids, City AM has learned.

The FTSE 100 bank is now in pole position to buy the entire Aldermore group, in a sale that would include both its bank and car finance lender, Motonovo, sources said.

South African lender Firstrand put Aldermore up for sale in April this year and received initial interest from around a dozen suitors.

The process has been narrowed down to its last few bidders, which are seeking to buy either parts of or the entirety of the bank. Analysts at RBC said they expect the group to fetch a price tag of between £1.1bn and £1.6bn.

Investec, which is dual-headquartered in the UK and South Africa, is among the final contenders circling the banking unit but is keen to avoid Motonovo, the group’s loss-making motor finance lender, sources said. Private equity firms Warburg Pincus and Cerberus had also submitted a joint bid for the company but have since pulled back from the deal.

Firstrand is leaning towards selling the group collectively in a single deal to Lloyds, the sources said.

Lloyds, Investec and Aldermore declined to comment.

Motor finance woes follow Aldermore

Motonovo is understood to have been a source of friction for some bidders. The car finance market has been in turmoil after the City watchdog set out a multi-billion pound compensation scheme earlier this year over historic missold loans.

Motonovo recognised a £153.2m charge in its latest accounts to pay for the redress scheme. This was more than double the £60.6m recorded the prior year.

The Supreme Court partially overturned a landmark ruling on car finance deals last year, rejecting claims that hidden commissions were automatically unlawful. But it found one customer’s undisclosed commission created an “unfair relationship”, leaving the door open for an industry-wide payout.

Firstrand confirmed it was selling Aldermore after voicing frustration at the Financial Conduct Authority’s compensation scheme. 

Lloyds owns the UK’s largest motor finance lender and has provisioned some £2bn for the ongoing mis-selling scandal.

A tie-up with Aldermore would allow the blue-chip banking group to beef up its standing in buy-to-let (BTL) mortgages, where it currently dominates 15 per cent of the market through its subsidiary BM Solutions.

Some 40 per cent of Aldermore’s £17bn loanbook also comes from the BTL market.

articles.title: Game on: How to make the most of game season
articles.summary:
Game season is well and truly underway across the UK. As cooks’ minds start to wander towards the turkey and goose, spare a thought for the partridge. Game has a bad rep: too metallic, too lean, too hard to cook. Growing up my mum – too embarrassed to turn down his gamey advances – used to take pheasants that were gifted to us by an eccentric local. She would try to disguise in chicken pies and curries, but we always knew. Teeth would crunch down in metal shotgun pellets and it tasted terrible. But when done well, it can steal the show. No wonder restaurants are stuffing their menus with squabs and grouse. 

Tomás Gormley, chef-owner of Cardinal in Edinburgh says: “Every year I do a partridge and bread sauce dish, usually with some sort of stone fruit. This year we’re getting some amazing damsons, so I’ll definitely incorporate them into that somewhere.

“I’m also growing some fantastic spaghetti squash and radicchio in our kitchen garden, so I’m excited about pairing those with game. I cook all the game we get at Cardinal over coals on the barbecue. I usually rest it in a tray of seasoned duck fat to keep it moist while cooking it slowly over the heat. Game is usually quite lean, so you need to be very careful when cooking it. Getting it right really pays off, though.”

Cooking royalty and Irish bon vivant Richard Corrigan’s partridge in a pear tree dish is an ideal as we shift into December. The gaminess of the bird works perfectly with fruit and warming ginger.

Spatchcock partridge with pears, quince and lentils

Partridges

2 partridges

For the Quince Puree

8 whole quinces

1 litre pear juice

200ml lemon juice

300g caster sugar

1 litre water

Pickled Pear

4x wax tip Williams pears

200g ginger

500ml litre water

250g caster sugar

250g Chardonnay vinegar

Puy Lentils

400g puy lentils

1x carrot

2x shallots

2 cloves of garlic

1 stick celery

Sprig of thyme

100ml white wine

Method

Start by making the quince purée. Bring to the boil lemon juice, pear juice, water and sugar. Peel, quarter, deseed and slice the quinces then place into the poaching liquid. Simmer until tender, strain and blitz. Add some of the poaching liquid back to the purée until the correct consistency is reached then pass through a sieve and chill.

Now make the pickled pear. Peel and finely julienne the ginger before blanching. Now make a syrup with the water, sugar and vinegar then add the blanched ginger. Peel, quarter and deseed the pears and finely slice. Steep the sliced pears into the hot ginger syrup and set aside.

Now turn to the puy lentils. Finely chop the shallot, carrot, garlic, thyme and celery and sweat in a heavy bottomed pan and cook until caramelised. Deglaze with white wine and cook out. Add the washed lentils to the pan and cover in water, bring to a simmer and cook for approximately 15 minutes making sure the lentils still have a bite. Leave the lentils to cool in the liquid.

To prepare the partridges, remove the wishbone with a small sharp knife. Then, using a sharp pair of scissors, cut along both sides of the spine and remove it. Lay the birds on a board with the breasts facing up, and press down on the middle of the breast to flatten them slightly. Season both sides of the birds well with sea salt.

Set the same pan over medium heat with a splash of oil, and lay the partridges in, skin side down. Once the pan is sizzling, reduce the heat to low and place a weight on top of the birds. Cook for 6-8 minutes, then flip the birds and turn off the heat.

Dice the chorizo and saute in butter, once coloured add the lentils along with some of the lentil cooking liquid. Adjust seasoning and finish with chopped parsley before serving up.

articles.title: St James’s Place sued by former partner firm Wellesley
articles.summary:
FTSE 100 wealth manager St James’s Place (SJP) has been hit with High Court legal action by one of its largest former partner firms, Wellesley Investment Management.

West Sussex-based Wellesley was previously one of SJP’s largest advice firms, operating as a self-employed practice within its partnership network.

The wealth advisory firm managed £1bn in funds and was once recognised as one of SJP’s largest practices by funds under management.

In July, Wellesley ended its relationship with SJP to join the UK network of the Swedish wealth management group Söderberg & Partners.

In its announcement, the firm said: “By joining the Söderberg & Partners network, we combine the personal relationships and tailored advice that define Wellesley, with the investment expertise, scale and innovation of an international organisation overseeing more than £100bn in assets under advice.”

At the time, reports said the advisory firm left the FTSE giant’s network around the same time as another SJP firm, Sheffield-based Prospera Wealth Management. The firm has since joined Söderberg & Partners Financial Planning.

Court action

On Wednesday, the High Court showed that Wellesley had instructed specialist disputes law firm Signature Litigation to file a case against St James’s Place Wealth Management plc, St James’s Place Management Services and St James’s Place Partnership Services.

SJP declined to comment. Wellesley was contacted for comment. It is understood that the case was filed with the Commercial Court, but the formal statement of case has yet to be served to the defendants.

In July, it was reported that SJP took a £1bn hit to net inflows in the first half of the year as investors pulled cash from its funds to dodge market volatility and a looming pension tax bill. Its net inflows declined from £3.8bn to £2.7bn in the first half of the year, in line with analyst expectations. The group pinned the decline on market uncertainty coupled with “impending changes” to the retirement and financial planning landscape.

articles.title: Dan Evans risks backlash by playing in Gazprom-funded Russia tennis event
articles.summary:
Davis Cup hero and former British No1 Dan Evans has risked criticism by coming out of retirement to play in a tennis tournament hosted in and funded by Russia.

Evans is among eight non-Russians in the 12-person field for the Northern Palmyra Trophies mixed doubles exhibition tournament taking place in St Petersburg from today until Sunday.

The event is being financed by Gazprom, the state-owned energy giant whose sponsorship of football’s Champions League was terminated by Uefa when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Russia remains a pariah in the sporting world as a result of its attacks on Ukraine, with its national teams and clubs banned in football, rugby union, basketball and athletics.

Evans, 36, retired from professional tennis after this year’s Wimbledon but agreed to dust off his racket for the Northern Palmyra Trophies. It is not known what fee he is receiving.

Other players taking part include Frenchmen Adrian Mannarino, 38, and Corentin Moutet, who was fined £30,000 for swearing seven times in a live BBC interview at Queen’s Club last year.

Former world top 10 players Janko Tipsarevic, of Serbia, and Alexander Bublik, who was born in Russia but represents Kazakhstan, and Russian Karen Khachanov are also on the bill.

Completing the line-up are Kamilla Rakhimova of Uzbekistan, Anastasia Potapova, who was born in Russia but now represents Austria, Elena Vesnina, Yulia Putintseva, Diana Shnaider and Anna Pushkareva.

Dan Evans’ career mixed controversy with glory

Evans has previously overcome controversy to become a popular figure in British tennis and part of the Great Britain team that won the Davis Cup in 2015.

His national funding was suspended aged 18 after he was pictured in a nightclub hours before a match at Wimbledon and cut altogether two years later for poor performance.

After re-establishing himself and helping Andy Murray lead Britain to Davis Cup glory he received a one-year ban from tennis in 2017 after testing positive for cocaine.

He rebuilt his career again, becoming British No1 in 2019, winning his first ATP Tour title in 2021 and reaching a career-high 21 in the world rankings in 2023.

In 2024 he played alongside Murray as the latter bowed out of professional tennis at the Paris Olympics and this summer hung up his own racket.

Russia has been creeping back into top-level sport, with the International Olympic Committee’s reinstatement in June paving the way for a team at the LA28 Games.

The country won a legal battle to be allowed back into international ice hockey just weeks ago, although the decision has been met with resistance by much of the sport.

articles.title: Chinese e-commerce giants could starve high streets of Black Friday boost
articles.summary:
Chinese retail giants like Temu and Shein could be the big winners from this year’s Black Friday, as high street shops are starved of “make or break” footfall, industry figures have warned.

Overseas e-commerce firms are able to avoid paying tax on any imports worth less than £135 as part of a tax loophole known as the ‘de-minimis’ threshold. Retailers have long campaigned for this rule to be scrapped, warning they face an uneven playing field. 

The British Independent Retailers Association, a trade body representing the high street, said it is “concerned” many UK shops will miss out on crucial Black Friday trading because Brits are opting to stay at home and order goods cheaper online.

Jeff Moody, the group’s chief operating officer, told City AM: “Overseas platforms start every sale with an advantage British retailers can’t match. Independent retailers can’t afford to slash margins the way the ultra-low-cost Chinese platforms do, and most don’t try. 

“They compete on expertise, service and being part of their community. But when the rules are tilted against them, good businesses lose sales they should be winning.”

He added that the so-called golden quarter – which includes Black Friday and the Christmas shopping period – “makes or breaks the year for many independents”.

Black Friday has always been a crucial period for retailers since the US tradition spread to the UK, but recent hikes to business rates and employment costs mean high street businesses need this extra revenue more than ever.

Moody added: “The money they take between now and Christmas carries them through the quiet months of January and February. If that trade doesn’t come, some will struggle to survive into the spring.”

The government has committed to closing the de-minimis loophole but this rule change will not come into force until October 2028 – having been accelerated from an initial deadline of March 2029. 

Long wait for tax crackdown

Dan Tomlinson, exchequer secretary to the Treasury, said when announcing the crackdown that the government would “tackle the unfair competition and dodgy businesses that are doing real damage to our high streets”.

But retailers have urged the government to move quicker, warning that recent clampdowns in the US and the EU mean that e-commerce firms are increasingly targeting UK shoppers because they now face higher taxes in these other markets. 

The value of Chinese parcel imports below the £135 threshold soared from £1.3bn to £5.3bn in the two fiscal years to 2025-26, according to recent HMRC data obtained by the Financial Times.

Tom Ironside, director of policy at the British Retail Consortium, said: “UK retailers have called for the same approach as the EU: tariffs on goods, alongside an administrative fee to cover the cost of customs. 

“The key difference is that the EU has put these measures in place already, while UK retailers will have to wait until October 2028 for action. That means two more years of inaction, increasing the risk that the UK becomes even more attractive to overseas online sellers.”

At the Budget last month, John Healey said online retailers will be made responsible for collecting VAT from the sellers which use their platforms, in a bid to equalise the tax burden between these firms and the high street.

These new rules will apply to all sellers whose annual revenue exceeds £90,000 but some tax experts have said this threshold should be dropped to zero. “Unless that happens these Chinese sham companies will find just another way around the rules,” said Tax Policy Associates founder Dan Neidle.

articles.title: Lloyds Bank hit with app outage on Black Friday
articles.summary:
Thousands of Lloyds Banking Group customers were locked out of their apps as shoppers rushed to cash in on Black Friday deals.

The banking giant – whose brands include Lloyds Bank, Bank of Scotland and Halifax – was battling its fifth technical glitch of the year after customers were shown an error message when trying to log in to their app.

When users tried to log onto their Lloyds app, a message read: “We know that some of our customers are having issues logging into online banking and our app.

“We are sorry about this and we’re working to have everything back to normal as soon as we can.”

The Downdetector – which tracks major website outages – showed a spike of over 4,000 registered issues for Lloyds early on Friday morning.

It also coincided with a “cyber incident” at the Department of Work and Pensions that forced the government unit to take some online services offline.

Lloyds has been contacted for comment.

Lloyds outages rack up

Earlier this year, the firm faced a “technical glitch” that left users of the bank’s app on Thursday morning seeing other users’ transactions on their mobile app.

Up to 447,936 customers of Lloyds and group subsidiaries saw rogue transactions across their accounts or had their data shared with other users.

Some 114,000 users were found to have clicked on other people’s exposed transactions that may have revealed sensitive information such as account details, national insurance numbers and payment references.

In a letter to the Treasury Select Committee, Lloyds chief executive of consumer relations Jasjyot Singh said the bank had made “good will” payments to over 3,600 customers, with compensation reaching north of £139,000.

Over the last month, UK regulators have ramped up pressure on banks to scale their cyber protections amidst growing threats from artificial intelligence and fraudsters.

articles.title: How AI agents are testing retailers on Black Friday
articles.summary:
Retailers are battling a new breed of fraud this Black Friday as AI shopping agents transform how consumers shop and pay online.

AI shopping activity is now 77 times higher than a year ago and 11 times higher than three months ago, according to fraud prevention firm Forter.

Meanwhile, British cybersecurity giant Darktrace found that daily Black Friday phishing volumes surged more than thirteenfold in the first three weeks of November, compared with October.

The seasonal increase was 29 per cent greater than last year, with AI introducing new vulnerabilities for shoppers and retailers alike.

Darktrace chief executive Ed Jennings described AI agents as a “new insider threat”, warning that businesses’ security capabilities were struggling to keep pace with adoption.

“It feels a little bit like the cloud rush of a few years back when cloud innovation got ahead of security and security had to catch up”, he said.

Margaret Cunningham, vice president of security and AI strategy at Darktrace, also warned that shopping assistants could recommend fraudulent sellers based on fabricated reviews.

“The shopper may see a recommendation without knowing how it was influenced”, she said.

Retailers face AI dilemma

The emergence of autonomous shopping tools, like Meta’s Muse – which landed in the UK this week – and OpenAI’s ChatGPT Wallet, is forcing retailers to rethink their business models.

Forter has identified more than 2,000 active fraud rings across the retailers it monitors, which collectively account for around $1.5 trillion in commerce.

“Like every time there’s a new technology, they will come up and try to find the vulnerabilities in it,” Michael Reitblat, chief executive of Forter, told City AM.

But retailers face a difficult trade-off between protecting themselves against fraud and capitalising on a potentially lucrative new sales channel.

While Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from shopping on its website in September, Walmart has embraced the technology, creating dedicated profiles for AI agents within customer accounts.

“If you block agents, they’ll just go somewhere else,” Reitblat said.

Smaller retailers could also benefit as AI erodes the advantage enjoyed by established brands with deeper advertising pockets.

“If you have a better product or a better service, whatever it is that you do, I think AI makes it easier for you to be found,” he added.

The trust gap

Despite the surge in activity, research from Salesforce found that only five per cent of UK shoppers have allowed an AI agent to make a purchase, although 75 per cent trust AI recommendations.

Visa’s recent experiment involving 22 personal shopping agents found that just 57 per cent of shopping trips resulted in a suitable purchase or recommendation.

The technology also raises unresolved questions over financial liability when an agent makes an unauthorised purchase or is compromised by criminals.

As a response, American Express has announced plans to protect eligible customers against purchases made by registered AI agents that contradict their instructions.

The challenge for retailers is particularly acute as MPs today called for tougher protections against misleading discounts and online scams.

Parliament’s business select committee has called on Andy Burnham to stop shoppers from being “bombarded” with misleading promotions, as the body criticised Amazon and John Lewis for refusing to co-operate with its inquiry.

As Black Friday kicks off, shoppers will be hoping to take advantage of hefty discounts at a time when consumer confidence is near a 10-year low. But MPs have said they are worried Brits are being taken advantage of.

articles.title: DWP takes services offline after cyber incident
articles.summary:
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has taken some of its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident, leaving some benefit claimants unable to access their accounts.

The government confirmed on Friday morning that it had shut down some services as a precaution, with Universal Credit claimants reporting difficulties signing into their online accounts.

A Number 10 spokesman added that there was no evidence that possible hacking was conducted by a “malicious actor” as they confirmed an investigation was “ongoing”.

““It’s a live and ongoing incident, and we’re working as quickly as possible to restore the services,” she said.

“There’s no evidence that it’s targeted at other departments.”

DWP is working with GCHQ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate the incident and restore services.

Officials stressed that regular benefit and pension payments would not be affected by the disruption.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department said.

“We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption.”

The government has yet to disclose the nature or scale of the incident, whether any personal data has been compromised or when it expects services to be fully restored.

DWP warns claimants over suspicious messages

The department, which is responsible for administering Britain’s welfare and state pension systems, urged those unable to access online services to try again later.

Universal Credit claimants typically use their online accounts to check payment dates, report changes in circumstances and communicate with their work coaches.

The DWP also reminded claimants to remain vigilant against potentially fraudulent messages.

“As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links,” it said.

The attack raises fresh questions over the resilience of Britain’s public sector digital infrastructure and the ability of government departments to maintain essential services during cyber disruption.

articles.title: Labour set for bitter internal clash over Rosebank approval
articles.summary:
Labour factions are battling over an impending decision on whether to allow Equinor and Shell to proceed with oil drilling at Rosebank in the North Sea.

Statements are being drawn up by backbenchers in the Labour Party to lobby the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh on her imminent decision, it has been reported.

One letter, signed by up to 96 Labour MPs, had written to Andy Burnham and Fahnbulleh demanding that the project is not given the go-ahead, dealing a blow to large energy companies waiting for about three years on a full ministerial decision, The Guardian reported.

Several MPs spoke publicly against Rosebank in a parliamentary debate earlier this month, including the former parliamentary private secretary Catherine Fookes, who organised the letter.

The letter said that approval would “permanently damage our climate credentials” and put the trust of some voters at risk.

“Polling is clear — in order to stand a chance of winning parliamentary majorities, maintaining our ‘progressive’ electoral base is imperative. Your new vision of hope has brought back voters from other progressive parties that we need in order to win the next election,” the letter said.

“However, approving Rosebank risks becoming an irreversible ‘point of no return’ for the party’s climate credibility, and risks alienating members of the electorate who have put their trust in our message of hope and positivity.”

Fahnbulleh’s Rosebank predicament

Aides in the government could also resign if the project is signed off by Fahnbulleh, who has been accused of co-ordinating a party rebellion against Rosebank. Allies of Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary who is now the foreign secretary, have spoken against the project.

A separate group of about 80 MPs support the project and could write a rivalling letter, Sky News reported. Some MPs, including the backbencher Henry Tufnell, have been publicly supportive of giving the project the green light. Some Labour MPs spoke in favour of Rosebank.

The crunch decision could have financial implications for the government given the Office for Budget Responsibility explicitly mentioned Rosebank in its assumptions on public finances in October.

Fahnbulleh will make the final call. She could turn the project down on environmental grounds and energy security, as much of the oil at Rosebank’s field is set to be exported.

John Healey and other Cabinet ministers are reportedly supportive of Rosebank due to extra tax income and job creation in Scotland. Healey travelled to Rosebank’s field in the North Sea when it was approved by the government before the Budget.

The unions GMB and Unite also back the project.

Fahnbulleh has previously said the decision involved a “tight process” and was “not a policy process”.

articles.title: Harry Brook-backed cricket startup Hitz valued at £12m ahead of £5m raise
articles.summary:
Harry Brook-endorsed British tech startup Hitz Cricket has been valued at £12m as it looks to raise a further £5m to fund its global expansion.

The company, which provides automated batting practice facilities for recreational facilities and elite training, operates 17 sites in the UK and Australia and is planning to open a further 16 across the country and in North America.

Hitz Cricket is close to reaching its £500,000 target on crowdfunding site Republic, which it will bolster with sums from seasoned, figures from the sport and private consortiums.

“We’re raising £5m across several phases: an angel round, the Republic Europe community campaign, and strategic partners,” founder Dom Reed told City AM. “The Republic campaign has already passed 80 per cent of its target.”

He added: “We’ve deliberately built a round that reflects our community. Alongside angel investors from the worlds of cricket and business, we opened up a crowdfunding round so our members, the people who actually play in our venues, can own a piece of Hitz.

“We raised over £400,000 in the private phase before the campaign even went public. We have term sheets out for a small number of small private groups to back the business in a significant way.”

International expansion

Hitz Cricket is working with Grant Thornton to identify suitable strategic partners to close the round and bring international scaling experience to the board in a non-exec role. Community backers won’t take board seats but will benefit from regular updates and investor perks.

England white-ball captain Brook is an athlete ambassador for Hitz and has created a workout designed to help budding cricketers hone their skills using the automated technology. The £12m figure is a pre-money valuation.

It comes as Hitz Cricket prepares to launch in five venues in North America: four in the US, including New Jersey, Maryland and North Carolina, and one in Ontario, Canada. This week the company announced plans to branch out into the Caribbean in a partnership with West Indies Cricket.

“The money will take Hitz global,” Reed said of the funding round. “It’ll fund our international roll-out through Project 2030, including our North America launch and the five-year Cricket West Indies partnership to bring Hitz across the Caribbean.

“It will also strengthen our UK estate and invest in our technology and member experience. Cricket has more than two billion fans, and we want Hitz to be how a new generation plays it.”

articles.title: Top Tory Griffith: I’ve got a screaming buy on the UK
articles.summary:
Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has said he has “got a screaming buy on the UK” as he backed the country’s economic prospects even as a critic of the government’s policies.

Griffith said the “fundamentals of this market – politics aside, noise aside” were “amazing”.

The Conservatives’ pick for Chancellor said investors had not taken enough account of businesses across AI, life sciences and advanced manufacturing.

“I’ve got a screaming buy on the UK. I think that the fundamentals of this market, politics aside, noise aside, the fundamentals are amazing,” he said.

“While people have chased the very voguish capital things like AI and semiconductors, actually the true strengths of the UK, which is a very diverse, investable business community, have often been overlooked.”

But Griffith also said that the UK was “not actually comfortable with the idea of people getting wealthy” in an interview with Wealth Club.

The shadow chancellor has doubled down on regulation faced by British companies at the same time as the Labour government has focused on improving rules faced by businesses, setting the two mainstream parties up for battles on regulatory costs.

Griffith suggests backing extra investment reliefs

Earlier this week, John Healey appointed William Sargent, a former film studio executive, to chair the Better Regulation Executive, receiving some backing from trade associations.

Yet the shadow chancellor wrote to Healey urging him to intervene on FCA rules around corporate reporting requirements.

He highlighted catering company Compass’ decision to leave the London Stock Exchange as a “concerning” event for UK markets.

After writing a letter to the City regulator’s chair Nikhil Rathi to tell him to drop incoming rules on sustainability reporting, Griffith told Healey that the government should drop “mandatory ethnicity or disability pay reporting burdens” and instruct the FCA to drop its own requirements.

“We have brilliant businesses and founders in the UK, but your failure to act at pace would be another hammer blow to Britain’s ability to compete with growing economies across the globe,” he said.

In the interview, Griffith warned that the reduction in income tax relief for venture capital trusts could be reversed by the Conservatives.

“I think in general, no piece of financial architecture is perfect, but that was a good one. It properly added extra money coming in, when we don’t have enough brilliant founders with enough capital chasing after them. And change these things at your peril.”

articles.title: Lloyds to capture most of £4bn prize from Bank of England shakeup
articles.summary:
Lloyds Banking Group is set to walk away with the biggest slice of a multi-billion-pound regulatory windfall after the Bank of England proposed a reduction of capital requirements on Britain’s domestic lenders.

UK banks are expected to collect around £4bn in freed-up capital headroom under the shakeup, roughly £1bn of which will flow straight to Lloyds, according to RBC analysis.

The proposed relief will allow domestically focused lenders to receive larger reductions, with capital requirements falling by 60 basis points at the likes of Natwest and Lloyds.

Capital requirements are the financial buffers regulators force banks to hold in reserve to absorb unexpected losses during an economic downturn. The funds cannot otherwise be lent out or returned to shareholders.

Because banks will only need to hold around 13p of capital against every £1 of risk-weighted lending, the £4bn release – combined with earlier leverage reforms – multiplies into roughly £175bn in theoretical lending firepower, according to the Bank of England,

“The FPC has assessed the calibration of domestic risk add-ons and decided they are too punitive,” Jefferies analysts wrote.

But the reduction still falls short of the £250bn trade body UK Finance lobbied for under a raft of reforms.

The Bank will consult on the changes in the first half of 2027.

Bank govenor ‘recoils’ at lending complaints

It follows a long-standing lobbying campaign by the industry, urging Threadneedle Street to lower the capital burden to spur economic growth.

“The picture is one, which I believe, is overly risk-averse and internationally uncompetitive,” UK Finance boss David Postings told a City audience earlier this year.

He added the system was “overly complex” with buffers that “overlap and confuse”.

The central bank’s Financial Policy Committee (FPC) said the proposals would make capital requirements “more proportionate, better targeted and – as a result – lower”.

It added: “These measures will free up further capacity to lend to UK households and businesses”.

But Bank governor Andrew Bailey confirmed, “it is for the banks to decide how they respond to these changes”.

Shares in Natwest and Lloyds popped around three per cent in the trading session when the Bank revealed the update.

But the FPC fired a warning shot for any future lobbying offensive, cautioning that further reductions in capital requirements would “risk financial instability” and “put long-term economic growth at risk”.

“I do recoil when I hear it said that banks can’t afford to lend,” Bailey told reporters following the FPC publication, as he pointed to a rise in lending while banks made bumper returns over the last year.

articles.title: Ofcom joins forces with Australian watchdog ahead of social media ban
articles.summary:
The UK’s digital watchdog Ofcom has announced a new partnership with Australia’s online safety regulator as Britain prepares to follow in the country’s footsteps by banning under-16s from social media.

The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the two regulators share intelligence, expertise and practical lessons from Australia’s implementation of the world’s first social media age restrictions.

It comes just a day after culture secretary Lisa Nandy warned the “jury is out” on whether Ofcom is capable of delivering on its expanding regulatory remit.

Ofcom chief executive Dame Melanie Dawes is leading a delegation to Australia this week, meeting policymakers and regulators to examine the country’s experience of enforcing age restrictions.

“Ofcom is working hard to ensure children are protected from day one of the new social media ban in the UK. That’s why this partnership is so important,” Dawes said.

“Australia’s experience will be invaluable as we prepare to enforce these new protections.”

The agreement will also strengthen cooperation on tackling online abuse, harassment and gender-based violence, alongside discussions over emerging harms associated with artificial intelligence.

Julie Inman Grant, Australia’s eSafety commissioner, said: “Online harms do not stop at national borders, and neither should our efforts to tackle them.”

Ofcom faces enforcement challenge

Britain’s social media ban, due to come into force in March, will prevent under-16s from accessing platforms including Instagram, Tiktok, Snapchat and Youtube.

Ministers are also considering extending restrictions to online marketplaces including Vinted and eBay over concerns their messaging functions could be exploited to groom children.

But questions remain over the practicalities of enforcing the ban, with evidence from Australia suggesting children have continued to access restricted platforms despite the legislation.

Ofcom last month identified four age verification methods it considers sufficiently reliable, including photo ID matching, facial age estimation, banking-based checks and digital identity services.

The proposals could see millions of adult social media users forced to verify their age, adding to the compliance burden facing technology giants operating in Britain.

The watchdog has acknowledged that circumvention cannot be eliminated entirely. Research from EE found that 42 per cent of young people plan to get around the ban by moving to apps outside its scope.

Speaking to Sky News on Thursday, Nandy said she was actively discussing Ofcom’s performance with its new chair, who had been brought in to “shake things up”.

The culture secretary previously admitted there was “a problem” with the watchdog’s ability to enforce online safety rules, warning that “laws are only as good as the ability to enforce them”.

Under the Online Safety Act, Ofcom can impose fines of up to £18m or 10 per cent of qualifying global annual turnover on companies that breach their obligations.

articles.title: Crack down on ‘fake discounts’ before next Black Friday, MPs urge
articles.summary:
MPs have urged the government to accelerate its crackdown on so-called fake discounts to ensure it protects shoppers by Black Friday next year.

Parliament’s business select committee has called on Andy Burnham to stop shoppers from being “bombarded” with misleading promotions, as the body criticised Amazon and John Lewis for refusing to co-operate with its inquiry.

As Black Friday kicks off, shoppers will be hoping to take advantage of hefty discounts at a time when consumer confidence is near a 10-year low. But MPs have said they are worried Brits are being taken advantage of.

The committee’s report said: “British consumers are losing billions because misleading prices, online scams and unsafe products are not being adequately prevented or punished. These risks go up in the run-up to Black Friday.”

Andy Burnham has pledged to crack down on misleading discounts and subscription traps, as part of his pledge to provide households with “everyday fixes”, but these new rules are still being consulted on so have not arrived in time for this year’s Black Friday.

Liam Byrne, chair of the committee, said: “By Black Friday next year, we want fake discounts explicitly banned, tougher penalties for those who break the rules and proper protection for consumers, however they pay.

“Honest retailers deserve a level playing field and British shoppers should be able to hunt for a bargain without having to hunt for the truth.”

Misleading prices cost shoppers £10.6bn in the year May 2024, according to the National Centre for Social Research. Consumer group Which? has claimed that only a fifth of the discounts during Black Friday in 2025 offered the cheapest price that year.

The committee invited consumer giants John Lewis, Amazon and TIkTok to give evidence to its investigation but they all declined to appear and explain how they protect shoppers, it said.

Discount rules ‘unreasonable’

The MPs have called on the government to set up a consumer protection plan within six months, propped up by a named minister, multiple targets and measurable results.

Byrne added: “At a time when millions of families are counting every penny in the run-up to Christmas, British shoppers are being bombarded with fake discounts, false promises and fraudulent offers.”

Sue Davies, head of consumer protection policy at Which?, said: “Clearer rules on misleading pricing would reduce the legal hurdles regulators face and help create a level playing field for businesses that price honestly.”

Existing crackdowns on discounting have proved unpopular among some retailers, which claim that they pose an undue burden on companies and make it difficult for them to give shoppers value for money.

Chris Wootton, the finance chief of Frasers Group, which has had adverts banned over allegedly misleading discounts, said in September that the existing rules pose “unreasonable and we say unlawful barriers in the way of vigorous price competition in the market”.

articles.title: Meaning, not money: Four rules that make or break new sports competitions
articles.summary:
Modern sport is obsessed with the future: innovation, disruption, new formats, new audiences. Yet paradoxically the things that often make sport matter are old-fashioned: records, rivalries, heroes and history.

It’s why starting a new sporting competition is such a difficult business. You can build it but – to paraphrase Field of Dreams – will they come? The last few weeks have shown the knife-edge of that gamble.

We’ve seen rugby’s inaugural Nations Championship and Uefa’s Nations League burst into life, while on the other side of the coin (and it’s a mighty big coin) LIV Golf has found a bunker it can’t escape from.

It got me thinking: it can’t just be luck, or funding. There must be some science to why some competitions succeed and others stutter. And increasingly that answer lies not in economics but in sociology. 

Before we start comparing apples with oranges, I should note that, of course, not all new competitions are the same.

You have creationary competitions that build something entirely new, often giving growing sports a competitive stage for the first time. Examples include the UFC, X Games and Premier Padel Tour. 

Then you have evolutionary competitions that take something familiar and give it a new environment. The Nations League and Nations Championship both fall into this category, so too the Laver Cup in tennis and football’s Club World Cup.  

Finally, you have revolutionary competitions. The IPL, Formula E, The Hundred, TGL, King’s League, LIV;  they are noisiest and most controversial but face the highest risk of failing. 

Despite these differences, they’re all trying to change fan behaviour. And their chance of success is not defined by money but meaning. 

Jeopardy, belonging, proof and lore

Meaning is everything in sport and it is an infuriatingly fragile thing for marketers to deal with. Hard to build and easy to break but, without it, new competitions don’t stand a chance.

The first challenge is jeopardy. For sport to mean anything, something needs to be on the line. Not just what you stand to win, but what you stand to lose. A trophy, a title, a place in the next round. 

LIV Golf’s organisers thought they were doing the right thing by creating the sport’s biggest financial prizes, but they failed to understand what any gambler will tell you: it’s also what you stand to lose that makes it matter. 

The second rule is belonging. People don’t just want to watch sport; they want to be part of it. This is what the IPL understood so brilliantly, giving cities their own teams and creating new loyalties. Similarly, the X Games gave a generation of action-sports fans a competition that reflected them and their culture. 

Belonging means a supporter is tying their fate to the supported. When they win the fan wins and vice versa. You can’t just invent that. It comes from a deeper social need, that a sporting team or individual becomes an extension of a fan’s own identity. 

The third principle is proof. Sport has meaning when that meaning is shared. Like money, it only has value if other people believe in it too. 

Sold-out stadiums and big broadcast deals help – one of the biggest coups for the Nations Championship was securing wall-to-wall coverage on ITV – but visibility is not the same as proof. 

Proof comes from how deeply people care. This is perhaps what King’s League and other influencer-led competitions struggle to understand. 

The final way to create meaning is through lore. By now we’re all familiar with the Drive To Survive effect, but while stories are powerful, legends are more so. 

Lore is not just about storytelling; it’s about history. Wales’s victory over New Zealand in the Nations Championship mattered because it was their first in a lifetime. 

This doesn’t mean new competitions can’t bring a freshness to sport, but if they can borrow from or tap into sporting lore then they are that much more likely to create the meaning that they need.

Most important facets are too often an afterthought

There they are; four rules to create meaning. Simple in theory, but perhaps less so in practice. And yet I suspect they’re often an afterthought when people set out to create a new sporting competition. 

The first conversation will usually be financial. How much do we need? Who’s going to invest? But if I was about to start a new competition, I would be focusing my energy more on meaning that money. 

Matt Readman is chief strategy officer at sports creative agency Dark Horses.

articles.title: As it happened: FTSE 100 compounds gains as markets brush off AI fears
articles.summary:
Welcome back to City AM‘s FTSE 100 liveblog.

UK stocks are set to hold their gains on Friday morning, after the FTSE 100 surged 1.7 per cent on Thursday. This increase, helped by banks and miners, came as markets appeared to cool after several days of AI sell-offs.
