articles.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
articles.summary:
Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.

Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.

The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.

CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK

Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.

Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.

Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.

Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.

For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’

Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.

When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.

Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.

The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: Apple tightens Mac security as AI agents seek your files
articles.summary:
Ever download an app on your Mac and click through the permission requests without giving them much thought? You're certainly not alone. But what if one of those approvals gave an AI assistant access to your private messages, financial documents or even files you thought were protected?

That's the concern behind Apple's latest Mac security controls. As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks on your computer, they're also requesting access to more personal information. And once you grant certain permissions, an app could potentially see far more than you intended.

Now, Apple is introducing new protections in macOS 27.3 that give you greater control over what these apps can access. The changes arrived in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, with the broader software release still to come. Here's what Apple is changing and why you may want to check your Mac's privacy settings now.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS

AI assistants have become increasingly useful, especially when you want help getting through a long list of tasks. An AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on your behalf. For example, you might ask an AI agent to organize your Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in your email. To complete those tasks, the software may request permission to access information stored on your Mac. That's where things can get uncomfortable. Some apps request a powerful macOS permission called Full Disk Access, which can give them access to nearly everything stored on your computer, including information from other apps.

Apple warns that an app with this permission can read or modify sensitive files. It may also be able to delete or export information without asking you again. And the potential exposure goes beyond documents. Another powerful permission, called System & App Protection Override, can allow an app to control your Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when you grant unrestricted access. That's a lot of trust to place in software, especially when an AI agent can take actions without asking you to approve every step.

Apple's upcoming update introduces several changes designed to make powerful permissions easier to understand. It also gives Mac owners more opportunities to limit access before an app starts working.

Apple is separating its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The change helps clarify when an app is requesting permission to bypass built-in protections. Apple is also introducing more detailed warnings about the information an app could access if you approve its request. Instead of clicking through a vague permission prompt, you'll have more information about what you're allowing.

One of the biggest changes involves Full Disk Access. Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting this permission will let you choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process, depending on their purpose.

For example, an AI tool helping you organize work documents may only need access to one folder. You could grant that limited permission while keeping other protected information off-limits. Apple is also introducing a more consistent process for granting these permissions. You'll select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods.

Another important addition gives you more control over how AI agents interact with other apps. When configuring System & App Protection Override, you can choose which apps an AI tool may control. For each approved app, you can select Ask First or At Any Time. Choosing Ask First means the AI agent must request permission before controlling that app. That extra confirmation may slow down some automated tasks, but it also gives you an opportunity to catch unwanted actions.

Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system. That could make it easier to recognize when software is acting on your behalf.

MAC MALWARE CAN HIDE COMMANDS IN YOUR ICLOUD CALENDAR

Apple's announcement follows growing scrutiny over how much information AI-powered software can access. In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission. Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. Separately, a security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information. OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported.

These incidents highlight the security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software. Even legitimate applications can create privacy risks when they receive broad access to personal information. Apple's response focuses on making those permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Importantly, the changes won't prevent you from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions.

There's something worth knowing before assuming the update will automatically protect everything on your Mac. Apple says permissions you've already granted will remain in effect after the update. The new approval experience primarily applies when apps request permissions going forward.

That means an AI app you installed months ago could still have access to information you previously approved. You'll need to review those permissions yourself if you want to change them. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality. This should help prevent legitimate tools from losing features they need to operate.

You can review your Mac's privacy permissions now, even before macOS 27.3 becomes widely available.

Steps may vary slightly depending on your version of macOS.

If you find an app with permissions it no longer needs, you can revoke its access. Depending on your macOS version, you may see a toggle or an option to remove the app from the permission list. For macOS 27.3: Select an app and click the Remove (−) button to revoke access. To replace broad access with a more limited permission, remove the app and add it again. When prompted, choose the specific protected folders or apps it needs.

Keep in mind that some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly. Removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

You don't have to stop using AI assistants to protect your information. A few precautions can help you take advantage of these tools while reducing unnecessary exposure.

When an app requests access to your files, consider whether it needs permission to browse your entire Mac. If the new macOS controls offer a Choose Folder or Choose Apps option, use it to limit the information the software can reach. You can adjust those permissions later if the app needs additional access.

If you're using macOS 27.3, look for the Ask First setting when granting an AI agent permission to control another application. This gives you another opportunity to review what the software wants to do. It's especially useful when an AI tool interacts with apps containing sensitive personal information.

Be careful when installing new AI agents, particularly from unfamiliar websites. We've previously reported how AI-related scams target Mac owners through convincing fake download pages. Stick with official developer websites or the Mac App Store whenever possible. Keep your installed apps updated to receive security fixes.

Your Mac includes built-in malware protection, but reputable antivirus software can add another layer of security. It can help detect malicious downloads and other threats, including malware disguised as legitimate AI tools. However, antivirus software can't reliably prevent an app from accessing information you've already given it permission to use. That's why reviewing your Mac's privacy settings remains important. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Even when an app has limited access to your files, you should understand how it handles information you choose to share. Check whether the developer stores your data or sends it to cloud servers. Apple's permission controls can restrict access to protected information on your Mac, but they don't replace an app's privacy policy.

An AI tool may have needed access to a particular folder when you first installed it. That doesn't mean it needs the same permission indefinitely. Periodically check Privacy & Security and remove access that no longer serves a purpose. This is particularly important for AI apps you rarely use.

If you're allowing an AI agent to organize or modify files, make sure you have a recent backup. An automated task could accidentally delete something important or change a document you wanted to keep. Apple's built-in Time Machine can automatically back up your Mac and help you recover files if something goes wrong. For step-by-step instructions, check out our guide on how to back up your computer.

I'm glad Apple is taking a closer look at how much access AI agents can have on our computers. These tools are becoming more capable, and I can see why people would want an assistant that handles repetitive work. But giving an app permission to see everything on your Mac seems like a steep price to pay for convenience. I particularly like the option to make an AI agent ask before controlling another app. That's a level of oversight I would want, especially when personal information is involved. My biggest concern is that previously granted permissions will remain active. Apple can introduce better warnings, but those warnings won't change the decisions you've already made. I'd encourage Mac owners to spend a few minutes reviewing their settings rather than waiting for the next update.

Would you trust an AI assistant with unrestricted access to your Mac if it could save you hours of work, or does the thought of software reading your private information cross a line? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: With Spain’s far right on the cusp of power, can women bail Sanchez out once again?

articles.title: French student protests: A 'very bizarre' government response

He recounts a police intervention last October and the case of a student facing trial for defending a classmate, and has the full support of several teachers. articles.summary: As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an authoritarian state?

articles.title: We’d be ‘stupid’ not to: Poland defends $300M military AI deal with Palantir
articles.summary:
Poland signed a five-year deal worth around $300 million with U.S. tech giant Palantir on Friday to expand the use of artificial intelligence across its armed forces.

Warsaw’s decision to adopt Palantir’s Maven system, already used by Ukraine and NATO, comes as European militaries grapple with how to strengthen their defenses against Russia while reducing their reliance on American technology.

“It would be stupid and wrong not to use it,” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters, crediting Palantir’s technology with helping Ukraine withstand more than four years of fighting Russia.

Maven uses AI to analyze military data, supporting everything from logistics to the identification of battlefield targets.

Palantir celebrated the deal on X, calling Maven “the vanguard of next-generation AI warfare” and saying it was proud to stand with Poland in defending a “sovereign Europe.”

The company, which has drawn criticism for its work with U.S. immigration authorities and the Israeli military, faced protests in Warsaw earlier this month over concerns about data security and technological independence.

“All the keys, servers and information are — and will remain — exclusively in the possession of the Polish Armed Forces,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said. 

Defense authorities in Denmark, Finland, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden already use Palantir software, though not all use Maven.

Some are seeking to reduce that dependence. The Dutch military said in late October it wanted a European alternative by 2028, while France and Germany agreed in July to explore developing their own defense software.

Poland’s deal is a national rollout of Maven, which allied militaries already use through NATO’s command structure, as European militaries try to strengthen their defenses while reducing reliance on American technology.

Kosiniak-Kamysz said he would have chosen a Polish supplier if one offered comparable capabilities. The Defense Ministry says it is developing two domestic systems, AIRON and NEFRYT, that could eventually replace Palantir’s tools. The minister suggested Poland could develop an alternative by the time the five-year deal expires.

This article was updated. Antoaneta Roussi contributed reporting.

articles.title: Meta’s UK rollout for Muse AI agent exposes it to more liability
articles.summary:
LONDON — Meta will be on the hook for more of Muse’s mistakes in the U.K. than in the U.S., according to a comparison of the AI agent’s fine print in both countries by POLITICO.

Following conversations with regulators, Muse’s terms of service give British consumers more scope to seek redress if the personal AI agent makes mistakes compared with users in the U.S.

The findings indicate the tech giant was willing to commit to meeting higher liability standards to gain access to the U.K. market, and show that tech companies and users will face different liability and consumer law rules as personal AI agents roll out globally.

Muse, an AI agent that takes actions on users’ behalf, was introduced in the U.K. this week — several months after its launch in the U.S. — following talks with British regulators.

The Competition and Markets Authority, which enforces consumer law in the U.K., said Meta had made changes to Muse’s terms of service in the U.K. following “weeks” of engagement to “make them fairer for consumers” and ensure they reflect U.K. consumer law.

Meta declined to comment on detailed regulatory discussions. It says Muse can lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping — but publicly acknowledges the tool “can and will still make mistakes.”

The AI agent, which is the first to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., can also make payments on behalf of users with their approval.

The U.S. terms of service cap liability at $250 except for claims “arising from Meta’s gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud.”

They absolve Meta of liability “to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law” for any losses or damages caused by Muse “taking any unintended, erroneous or unauthorized action.”

In the U.K. there is no financial cap and a narrower list of exceptions to Meta’s liability applies only where the company has “acted with reasonable skill and care / professional diligence.”

Under U.K. consumer law, this standard is automatically implied into contracts for services between a business and a consumer. How U.K. consumers would fare in practice when seeking redress for any problems caused by personal AI agents is yet to be tested in court.

Since its debut in the U.S., Meta staffers have reportedly raised concerns internally about “undesired actions” by the agent, from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases. (A Meta spokesperson said these were “isolated incidents.”)

The CMA said it expects Muse to be the first of many personal AI agents to come to the U.K. and has invited users to report any issues they experience with personal AI agents.

Other British regulators are also watching closely. The Financial Conduct Authority said in a statement that as AI agents become capable of making transactions, payments and investment decisions, companies developing and deploying them “must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply.”

It also highlighted that a broad Consumer Duty could also apply to regulated firms’ use of AI agents, and that all companies must decide carefully whether they should accept payments initiated by an agent.

As well as contract law, consumer law, negligence and sector-specific regulation, users of AI agents may soon also be able to seek redress through product liability laws.

The Law Commission is reviewing the U.K.’s product liability laws and has proposed extending the definition to software, including AI. Doing so could make firms developing or deploying AI agents strictly liable for certain types of harm they cause.

articles.title: Asia-Pacific trade bloc opens accession talks with UAE, Philippines and Indonesia
articles.summary:
LONDON — Trade ministers from the Trans-Pacific Partnership launched accession talks with the UAE, Philippines and Indonesia on Friday.

The 12-nation trade alliance, also known as the CPTPP, agreed to establish three working groups to handle the negotiations, which could lead to its biggest expansion to date.

Countries joining the alliance must commit to sweeping tariff liberalization as well as opening up digital trade.

Accession talks with Uruguay, which have been running since early this year, are well advanced and could “potentially” be concluded early next year, a diplomat granted anonymity to discuss the plans told POLITICO.

Trade ministers are meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, for the 11th CPTPP Commission meeting, hosted annually by a rotating chair.

The U.K. became the first country without a Pacific coastline to join the bloc in 2024. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico and Singapore were among its founding members in 2018. Decisions are taken by consensus.

The U.K. is expected to sign a trade deal soon with the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the UAE. But London has yet to strike trade deals with the fast-growing Indonesian and Philippine economies.

Negotiations with the three nations “are all complicated and will require serious effort to get across the line,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation think tank. “This includes capacity building for some applicants to make certain that everyone is clear on what the CPTPP requires, as well as careful work to ensure that member concerns are addressed.”

The bloc is emerging as a “Plan B” as efforts to reform the World Trade Organization falter. China, Taiwan, Ecuador, Ukraine, Cambodia and Argentina have also applied to join.

articles.title: The man who coined ‘Brexit’ likes the sound of ‘Breturn’ and ‘Brejoin’
articles.summary:
LONDON — The political strategist credited with first using the term Brexit says it’s too early to predict slogans for a future referendum — but rates Breturn and Brejoin as potential portmanteaux.

Peter Wilding, a consultant based in Brussels, told POLITICO that the political landscape has shifted since 2016 when Brits voted to leave the EU and that pro-EU campaign rhetoric will have to change to keep up.

His comments come as U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reopens the conversation on Britain’s relationship with Europe, and campaigners on both sides of the debate regroup in preparation for a potential second fight over bloc membership.

Since arriving in Downing Street, Burnham has argued that Brexit “has not worked” as he tees up tighter ties with the EU. He has said that he hopes to rejoin within his lifetime — but insisted Monday that it would be “unthinkable” to do so without a referendum.

“If you’re looking for something catchy, there’s a couple of options: Let’s Breturn or Brejoin,” Wilding said when asked what the moniker for a future campaign should be. “But really, Burnham doesn’t want to go back to the past, he wants to go to the future, and the faces and arguments of 2016 will be dumped.”

“There will be a tonal change where Burnham caters his argument towards the younger vote and the business vote — seizing these cohorts will be vital to electoral success,” the strategist added.

Wilding coined Brexit in 2012 when he penned an article on Britain’s place in Europe.

“Unless a clear view is pushed that Britain must lead in Europe at the very least to achieve the completion of the single market, then the portmanteau for Greek euro exit might be followed by another sad word, Brexit,” he wrote for news outlet Euractiv , now known as Rapporteur. His writing is cited as the earliest evidence of the word Brexit in the Oxford English Dictionary.

The term was subsequently adopted as the accepted shorthand for the U.K. leaving Europe and was plastered on buses and billboards during the 2016 referendum campaign on Britain’s membership.

Having a snappy way of encapsulating the Vote Leave argument — and catchy slogans to go alongside — was crucial in building the campaign in the public imagination, Wilding said.

“The Take Back Control control slogan was an absolute winner.”

As Burnham gears up to set out different options for the U.K.-EU relationship, Wilding argued that the British prime minister has already got the upper hand on the opposition by co-opting the winning slogans of the past.

“Burnham has found the two best weapons from the 2016 campaign: take back control and immigration, and he has occupied that territory,” he said, pointing to the Labour leader’s party conference speech in September .

The PM told supporters in Liverpool: “The British Right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place.”

Wilding said that Burnham’s gradual approach to deepening Britain’s ties with Brussels is “flushing out” the opposition — who he claimed look “splutteringly indignant” when they trot out 2016-era arguments that have been disproved.

“Burnham is tackling the immigration argument head on,” Wilding said. “He can say you won that referendum on immigration and the Boriswave threw your credibility away and because of that you don’t have an argument to make” — a term coined by the online right to describe the increase in migration under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s Conservative government following the pandemic.

Nigel Farage, a key architect of the campaign to pull the U.K. out of the EU, announced Wednesday that he is launching a new effort Keep Britain Out.

“There will be a lot of online battling,” Wilding said. “But the only leader is Burnham himself, and what he says and does will affect the development of the Get In and Stay Out campaigns.”

On the question of whether the public is ready for another full-blown campaign, the Brexit-coiner said: “I don’t think they are. I think we are in the team talk period before the match begins and anything can happen in the next year.”

articles.title: Dépendance aux Big Tech américaines : où en est la France par rapport à ses voisins européens ?
articles.summary:
BRUXELLES — Même si l’UE est unie dans sa volonté de réduire sa dépendance aux technologies américaines, chaque Etat membre devra se débrancher de son côté — et certains auront bien plus d’efforts à fournir que d’autres.

Une étude menée par des chercheurs finlandais a mis en évidence de grandes disparités dans le degré de dépendance des Etats européens envers Amazon, Microsoft et Google pour les services publics numériques destinés aux citoyens.

“Cette variation n’est pas aléatoire, elle est systématique”, explique Vili Lehdonvirta, professeur de politique technologique à l’université finlandaise Aalto et coauteur du rapport.

Les chercheurs ont analysé les sites web gouvernementaux de 158 pays — notamment les portails permettant aux citoyens de trouver des informations, de déposer des demandes et d’effectuer des démarches administratives — afin d’évaluer dans quelle mesure ceux-ci dépendent des trois géants de la tech américaine.

Au sein de l’UE, Malte, la Finlande et l’Irlande affichent les parts les plus élevées de services publics nationaux hébergés par des hyperscalers américains : respectivement 78,5%, 56,1% et 45,8%.

En revanche, le taux estimé pour la France est de 9,3%, comparé à 2,9% pour l’Allemagne.

La publication de cette étude intervient alors que l’UE négocie actuellement un projet de législation qui obligerait les administrations publiques à revoir leurs achats de solutions digitales américaines, dans un contexte marqué par les menaces répétées de Washington contre les politiques numériques de Bruxelles, de tentatives locales de se passer des services américains et les récentes pannes ayant affecté des outils informatiques très répandus.

Selon l’étude, Bahreïn présente le plus fort degré de dépendance au monde, les services américains hébergeant 81% des sites étudiés, tandis que la Russie et la Chine ne comptent aucun site public lié aux trois géants de la tech.

Les chercheurs ont constaté que les disparités dans le recours aux Big Tech tendent à être liées à la taille d’un pays et au coût du travail.

“L’explication est d’ordre économique : dans un grand pays, le marché domestique est mieux à même de soutenir des alternatives ou des technologies nationales, qui impliquent des investissements importants et des économies d’échelle élevées”, a détaillé Vili Lehdonvirta.

Pourquoi la taille compte

En Europe, la carte de la dépendance aux technologies américaines suit des tendances similaires, reflétant la taille du marché et le niveau de revenu. Cependant, elle est également plus contrastée en raison d’un ensemble hétéroclite de choix nationaux qui complique les efforts de l’UE visant à réduire ces dépendances stratégiques.

“Dans l’ensemble, on a cette configuration où les petits Etats membres ont recours au cloud américain et pas les grands Etats membres”, a décrit Vili Lehdonvirta. “Le cloud est un exemple de technologie qui nécessite un investissement initial important, et ensuite, plus on opère à grande échelle, plus elle est efficace.”

La méthodologie de l’étude présente certaines limites pour évaluer le degré de dépendance globale, car elle se concentre uniquement sur l’hébergement des services nationaux destinés au grand public, et non sur les systèmes locaux ni sur l’utilisation plus large de la technologie au sein de l’administration. Par exemple, Vili Lehdonvirta indique que les entités municipales — tels que les conseils d’école ou les systèmes de billetterie des piscines — sont plus susceptibles de recourir à des technologies américaines, la souveraineté numérique ne relevant pas de leurs compétences.

La taille et les revenus ne font pas tout non plus : les choix politiques déterminent également si les pays développent ou non des fournisseurs nationaux.

Au Royaume-Uni — la cinquième puissance mondiale —, 50,9% des sites gouvernementaux dépendent de technologies américaines, selon l’étude. Vili Lehdonvirta rappelle que l’exécutif britannique “a décidé, il y a environ quinze ans, de mettre le paquet sur le cloud dans le cadre d’une directive du gouvernement s’appliquant à tous les ministères et agences gouvernementales”. En l’absence d’alternatives nationales, “très rapidement, tout a migré vers le cloud américain. Aujourd’hui, il serait difficile de revenir en arrière, même s’ils le souhaitaient”, souligne-t-il.

De nouvelles règles à venir

La publication de cette étude intervient alors que les responsables politiques à Bruxelles débattent pour savoir où fixer les limites : les nouvelles règles proposées — dans le Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) — devraient-elles obliger les administrations publiques à réaliser des tests de souveraineté et à se tourner vers des alternatives européennes pour les secteurs les plus sensibles, ce qui pourrait évincer les géants américains de la tech ?

Rien que dans le secteur privé, les entreprises européennes dépensent environ 330 milliards d’euros par an en services cloud et logiciels américains, ce qui confère à la tech américaine une part de marché estimée à 83% selon une étude de 2025.

Mais les Etats membres n’ont pas tous intérêt à des règles strictes en la matière. Cela dépend en partie s’ils ont ou non des fournisseurs nationaux prêts à rivaliser.

Josh Kallmer, directeur des affaires internationales chez Zoom, dont le siège est aux Etats-Unis, estime pour sa part que l’échelon européen est le bon niveau pour agir, car il permettrait d’éviter des règles différentes dans chaque pays. “Cette divergence supplémentaire affecte une entreprise comme la nôtre”, a-t-il déclaré lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO. “Chaque restriction supplémentaire mise en place a un impact beaucoup plus important sur la liberté de choix dans les pays de taille moyenne et les petits pays.”

Les négociateurs du CADA en sont pleinement conscients. “Nous devons essayer de mettre en place un cadre clair afin que les 27 pays aient la même interprétation de la loi, car, en fin de compte, le but est de faciliter la tâche des PME en Europe”, dit Diego Solier, eurodéputé membre des Conservateurs et réformistes européens, qui est l’un des principaux négociateurs sur ce dossier.

Pour le coauteur de l’étude, Vili Lehdonvirta, ce texte risque de rater sa cible s’il ne répartit pas plus équitablement les coûts et avantages au sein de l’UE.

“Le coût de la mise en conformité de cette politique pèse principalement sur les petits Etats membres, tandis que ses avantages, à savoir l’augmentation de l’activité économique, profitent surtout aux grands Etats membres”, développe-t-il. “Si nous ne disposons d’aucun mécanisme de partage des charges, le résultat final sera similaire à ce que nous observons actuellement, c’est-à-dire une sorte de tentative timide qui n’oblige pas vraiment qui que ce soit à agir.”

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

articles.title: ‘Islam is Sharia’: Germany’s far-right leader attacks Le Pen on Muslims and Europe
articles.summary:
BERLIN — Alice Weidel sees her far-right Alternative for Germany as the country’s new mainstream party. That doesn’t mean she’s moderating her message.

In a wide-ranging interview, the co-leader of the AfD — Germany’s most popular party — called for the departure of millions of migrants and accused Germany’s Central Council of Jews of taking its marching orders from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats.

She also took aim at Marine Le Pen, accusing the far-right French presidential candidate of isolating her own party on the European right by bashing Germany.

“Yes, I’m keeping my fingers crossed for Ms. Le Pen,” Weidel said during an interview with a new weekly video podcast from WELT published Friday. WELT, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

But Weidel bristled at Le Pen’s call this week for a “Europe of nations” to replace a “German Europe.” The leader of France’s far-right National Rally party had “perhaps misunderstood something, or doesn’t see how the money flows,” Weidel said, referring to Germany paying the largest portion of the EU budget.

The relationship between the two parties has been cold since Le Pen cut ties with the AfD in 2024, after one of the AfD’s leading politicians told an Italian newspaper that not every SS member was automatically a criminal. 

Among Europe’s “patriotic” parties, “it is not the AfD that is isolated, but increasingly the National Rally, if it carries on like this,” she added.

Weidel also rejected Le Pen’s contention in a television appearance in October that Islam, unlike Sharia, is compatible with the French Republic: “Islam is Sharia and Sharia is Islam.” Le Pen has worked to rid the party of the racist and antisemitic reputation it developed under her father, Jean-Marie, who was convicted multiple times for racist comments and downplaying the Holocaust.

On the subject of expelling migrants from Germany, Weidel outbid her AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla, who recently put the number of people who should leave Germany at 2.6 million. 

“Frankly, the number is much larger,” she said, and listed whom she meant: the roughly 250,000 people already obliged to leave the country as well as violent offenders, Islamists and others who “hang around in our social hammock, live an easy life here and don’t integrate.” 

She added those whose protection she would revoke once the reason for fleeing no longer applies — “completely, entirely, all” 900,000 Syrians, all Afghans and, after a peace deal, 1.1 million Ukrainians. 

On Ukraine, Weidel doubled down on her claim that Kyiv had already lost the war. If she were in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s shoes, she would recommend “immediately flying to Russia and sitting down at the table with Putin.” She added: “I would do it.”

Weidel dismissed the suggestion that a Russian victory would trigger another wave of refugees heading west. “There will be no refugee movement. Quite the opposite,” she said, arguing that Ukrainians in Germany would return home once peace was established “because they are needed there.”

Weidel was more evasive on the subject of Israel. 

Asked about a now-deleted post by AfD lawmaker Kay Gottschalk stating there is no “right to exist” for any nation, Weidel called it “botched.”

Asked directly whether Israel has a right to exist, she said, “As a German party, what befits us first and foremost is defending Germany’s sovereignty. That is in our national interest.” Then, “to answer your question directly”: anyone who looks at the AfD’s motions in the Bundestag over the past ten years “will see who stands at Israel’s side.” The AfD, she added, is “the only and last protective power of Jewish life in Germany.”

Asked why, then, the Central Council of Jews in Germany warns against her party, Weidel claimed the organization had been politicized by the CDU.

“It is permanently being used as a weapon against the AfD,” she said, offering no evidence.

Council President Josef Schuster has repeatedly warned that an AfD government would endanger Jewish life in Germany, citing the party’s positions on religious practices and its politicians’ remarks about the Nazi era. The Council did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a statement provided to POLITICO after publication, Schuster described Weidel’s allegation as “absurd.” 

“For years, the AfD has been searching for a fig leaf for its resentment-laden politics, while at the same time seeking to restrict freedom of religion and to destroy the consensus on the politics of remembrance,” he said. “The Jewish community in Germany will not provide it with that fig leaf.”

In September, Weidel declared that the AfD had supplanted the Christian Democrats as Germany’s traditional people’s party — meaning a party with broad appeal across society.

For all her attacks on the Christian Democrats, Weidel made clear she was still open to working with them. The CDU, which she no longer considers a center-right party, was “destroying itself behind the firewall,” she said, referring to the longstanding agreement by Germany’s establishment parties not to work with the far right. 

Her hand, she said, remains “outstretched.”

UPDATED: This article was update on Nov. 11 with a comment from Schuster.

Marc Felix Serrao is a Global Reporter with The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network and co-host of “Zur Wahrheit gehört” (“Part of the Truth”), a new weekly video podcast from WELT.

The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

articles.title: Wie der Rentenstreit die Koalition spaltet
articles.summary:
Listen on

Spotify

Apple Music

Amazon Music

Die Rentenreform steht auf der Kippe. Ein Kompromissvorschlag der Union zur abschlagsfreien Rente nach 45 Beitragsjahren lehnt die SPD ab, in der Union wächst der Frust. Rasmus Buchsteiner ordnet den Streit um die Respektrente ein und wie das gesamte Milliardenprojekt weiter gefährdet ist.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview erklärt Pascal Reddig, CDU-Abgeordneter und Mitautor des abgelehnten Papiers, wie es nun weitergehen soll. Er macht deutlich, warum ein Scheitern der Reform fatale Folgen hätte und ob es in der verfahrenen Situation überhaupt noch eine Chance auf Einigung gibt.

Auf EU-Ebene geht derweil der Kampf um den künftigen Finanzrahmen weiter. articles.title: Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans
articles.summary:
LONDON — Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned governments need to reassure the public about the benefits of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models, amid rising fears the technology is advancing at a pace beyond human control.

As the U.K. prepares to take over the G20 presidency, Bailey backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s plan to put AI at the heart of the country’s plans.

But the U.K. central banker said lawmakers, not regulators, would have to set the guardrails for the technology.

“It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England.

With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI.

U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as “super intelligence.”

Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency.

The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system.

With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves.

But the governor argued it was reasonable for the public to ask what the benefit is from the rapid growth of a technology which could be used to blow holes in the financial system, but also order the Christmas shopping.

“The public needs to trust this technology,” he said. “There needs to be greater transparency, explanation of what the things do, how they do it, what we’re doing.”

He added: “It’s sensible to come at it from that angle and say, we’ve got to have stronger government understanding, stronger government coordination on this stuff. Regulation may follow it.”

The U.K. central banker is acutely aware of the threats the new technology could bring to the financial system. The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee report on Thursday spelled out risks including increasingly interconnected and opaque financing that could spread the pain should a potential stock market AI bubble burst.

But Bailey said he would put himself in a camp of people who want AI to succeed to improve productivity and well-being.

“But it has to be under human control,” he said. “We want AI to be used by humans, as it were.”

articles.title: Ukraine cajoles allies to keep Putin’s athletes out
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — Kyiv is stepping up its bid to keep Russian athletes out of global sports tournaments.

“We cannot allow international sport to become the weak link in the democratic world,” Ukrainian Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi told POLITICO from Brussels, where he met EU sports ministers, as legal and political momentum builds for Russian competitors to return.

International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry has said athletes should not pay for governmental actions; top sporting organizations have eased restrictions instituted in 2022 after the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion began; and a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling overturned ice hockey’s ban on Russian teams.

Ukraine has near-unanimous EU backing for keeping Russian athletes out of European sport, and wants the bloc’s new visa ban on Moscow’s combatants also applied to soldiers who compete on national teams, Bidnyi added.

With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics on the horizon, the dispute is becoming a test of who’ll shape Russia’s return to world sport: governments, or federations and courts. Kyiv is desperate for Europe to coordinate its response before more restrictions are lifted.

Bidnyi said he presented three demands to EU sports ministers on Nov. 20: a ban on Russian symbols; verified neutral status for athletes; and funding cuts for federations that let Russians compete. He added that the proposals found “wide support.”

“I have heard no voice against it,” Bidnyi said. Asked whether all 27 EU countries are on board, he said that “almost all of them” had expressed willingness to make it a common position.

No propaganda in sport

On Monday, the European Commission proposed barring Russian teams and athletes from competing in the EU, which would also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European sports and cultural associations. The sanctions package needs the approval of all 27 member countries.

In addition, seven EU countries had written to European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the sanctions package was presented asking for tougher visa rules on Russian nationals.

The countries wanted the Commission’s guidelines on visa applications by Russians to prevent nonessential travel, including to sporting events, rather than wait for a revised Visa Code that is not expected before the first quarter of 2027. They also encouraged fellow EU countries not to grant visas to Russian or Belarusian athletes.

Bidnyi said his three points are designed to stop Russia from using sport for propaganda, while Moscow maintains a relentless bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.

The first measure is a ban on Russian symbols, such as flags or the national anthem. “It’s unacceptable that the anthem of a country that kills peaceful people in Europe today sounds in such a cheerful manner in European arenas,” he said.

A photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik showing Vladimir Putin meeting young ice hockey players while visiting the VOLGA Arena multifunctional sports complex in Nizhny Novgorod on Aug. 28, 2026. | Kirill Zykov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

The second is to make “neutral athlete” status something that is actually verified. “The neutral status should be maintained by detailed checking,” Bidnyi said. “We must check all aspects.”

The third is money. Bidnyi pointed to the new EU restriction on Erasmus+ funding — the bloc’s main program for education, training, youth and sport — for organizations that allow Russian state symbols, calling it a “first concrete result.” He wants the same model widened to organizations that let Russians use sport as a “tool of propaganda,” whether or not symbols are involved.

Bidnyi also raised the issue of soldiers that have become athletes, which touches the EU’s newest migration measures. The Commission’s visa guidelines, published this week alongside the sanctions package, tell national authorities to refuse visas to anyone who has served in Russia’s armed forces and fought in the war.

Bidnyi said the International Paralympic Committee has tolerated combatants taking part in its events, and that Russia is now trying to put soldiers who fought in Ukraine on its Paralympic teams. He called that “absolutely unacceptable.” Europe, he said, already refuses visas to combatants, and “it should be like this.”

The IPC said it has no rules barring former soldiers from competing, pointing to the movement’s origins in rehabilitating injured war veterans after World War II.

Nor is it its role, the IPC added, “to make moral judgments on which injured soldiers should or should not be allowed to compete.” It said former soldiers from countries including the U.S., Britain, Iraq, Bosnia and Iran have competed, and that it expects more at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The IPC said its responsibility is to decide which national Paralympic committees and athletes are eligible and to enforce its conduct rules. It said accreditation for the Games is the final decision of the organizing committee and national authorities, which handle security and background checks. Their organization’s answer did not mention Russia or Ukraine.

Russia’s sports minister, who the EU has also sanctioned, stated in September that more than 70 war veterans were already on national teams. Bidnyi also alleged that the Russian Union of Martial Arts recruits on behalf of units fighting in Ukraine and trains drone operators, and said that should be prohibited.

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Bidnyi’s assertions about Russia’s military recruitment and wider propaganda strategy.

Ice hockey backlash

Sporting institutions, however, are gradually moving toward Russian reinstatement.

On one side of the confrontation, Bidnyi said, are governing bodies, courts and federations, which are “gradually opening the door to Russians hiding behind claims of neutrality.”

His primary example is the Oct. 30 decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn the International Ice Hockey Federation’s ban on Russian teams for the 2026-27 season. “The hockey case is the most outrageous example of Russian influence,” Bidnyi said.

Russian Alexander Ovechkin celebrates during the charity hockey “Match of the Year” between Russian players of the National Hockey League and the Kontinental Hockey League at the CSKA arena in Moscow on July 13, 2025. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images

Asked for comment, CAS said that the case, brought by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the IIHF, “was decided on a strictly legal basis” and that it is not aware of any circumstance that could have affected the panel’s independence.

Ultimately, that ruling set off a backlash. Finland, Sweden, Czechia, Norway, Austria, Denmark and Latvia have said they will play at next May’s men’s world championship in Germany but not against Russia — which means almost half of the 16 teams are refusing to face Russia. Canada’s government said Russia will not be allowed to play at the world juniors there next month.

Sponsors are also balking, with Skoda, the tournament’s main sponsor, saying it will reassess its backing. The IIHF says it still disagrees with the ruling.

Sanctions have also been lifted in gymnastics, weightlifting and chess, and the international ski federation has cleared more than 400 Russian and Belarusian athletes and support staff to compete as neutrals this season.

Bidnyi expects more of the same. The IOC’s decision to reinstate the Russian Olympic Committee, he said, “has set a dangerous precedent. International federations may now begin lifting restrictions one after another, hiding behind the autonomy of sport.”

Moscow, Bidnyi said, will keep going back to CAS and present every readmission as a propaganda win, with Putin personally overseeing the effort.

On the other side, he said, are governments, which can take a “principled stand” and refuse to let Russian representatives or the symbols of an aggressor state onto their territory. Russian participation “has long ceased to be merely a matter of sporting regulations,” he said. “It is a question of national security.”

The next chance to build a common position is a meeting of sports ministers in Tallinn in January. Bidnyi said it could bring in non-EU countries such as Canada and Norway, which have already taken firm action.

articles.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
articles.summary:
A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669

Science History Images/Alamy

Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick?

For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Book Club

Sign up to newsletter

The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce.

Advertisement

If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet, money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world.

The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia, the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X, part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. In it, the recipe suggests using the “urine of a small child”, although today our understanding of the chemical reaction that creates the effect means we know water is a better alternative.

The 28 best popular science books of 2026

From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list

Fast-forward a thousand years, and the mass use of urine was commonplace around the world. It was still used for laundry and leatherwork, but was now also part of the burgeoning gunpowder industry. One of the key ingredients of this game-changing superweapon, the origins of which lie in Chinese herbal medicine, is saltpetre, or potassium nitrate. This was gathered from nitre beds, stinking manure heaps mixed with potash and mortar, all moistened with urine to claim the nitrates. This method, used from Europe to Japan, continued well into the 19th century; during the US Civil War, the Confederacy was using urine to keep its guns firing.

But perhaps urine’s greatest contribution came from alchemy. By the 17th century, just as the printing press and improvements in lenses and glassware had finally begun to usher in the scientific method, the old practices and beliefs that blended experiment, philosophy, religion and misunderstanding of the ancient world had their greatest triumph. In 1669, an alchemist in Hamburg, Hennig Brand, was searching for the philosopher’s stone using 1500 gallons of fermented urine he had collected in his basement. To Brand’s astonishment, the concentrated urine at the heart of his experiment began to glow. Brand kept his accomplishment secret for years, but unable to take the next step and turn metals into gold, he eventually sold the recipe to a friend and the discovery was shared with the world. Brand hadn’t performed a magic trick, but isolated phosphorus – the first chemical element to be discovered in modern times.

Today, urine still plays a critical role around the world, particularly in medicine, where it is a source of biomarkers used in diagnostic tests, and was even the original source of drugs such as human chorionic gonadotropin and follicle-stimulating hormone for fertility treatment. As Emperor Vespasian said almost 2000 years ago, money doesn’t stink – and nor do the benefits of the amber liquid we all produce every day.

Kit Chapman is the author of The Age of Alchemy, the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

articles.title: Read an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman
articles.summary:
The New Scientist Book Club is reading The Age of Alchemy in December

“A handful of lime and another of sulfur in fine powder.

Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child.

Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood.

Advertisement

Decant this properly, and use.”

Unknown, Leiden Papyrus X, c. 300 CE

In 1827, amid the dark, silent balm of an Egyptian night, a graverobber pulled a treasure from the sands. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements.

For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it.

The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway.

Free newsletter

Sign up to Book Club

Sign up to newsletter

When d’Anastasy wasn’t trading – or rescuing enslaved girls during the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire – he ran a side-hustle, “procuring” relics from Ancient Egypt and selling them to the salons of Europe: statues to the British Museum in London; rings and jewels to the Louvre in Paris; even a pair of sphinxes that still sit on the banks of the Neva River in St Petersburg. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands.

Among the Leiden trove was one of the most remarkable finds in history: a papyrus scroll with a list of recipes, each with crystal-clear instructions written in Greek. While we have damaged cuneiform tablets and later copies of older works, the Leiden Papyrus X, written around 300 CE, is the oldest surviving alchemy book in history. It is a guide for Egyptian artisans to create wondrous riches, seemingly out of nothing. There are methods on how to polish silverware, cheap alternatives for making knock-off purple robes, and how to create gold lettering by mixing saffron and tortoise bile. These are all real instructions, and all recipes that work (even if, today, there are cheaper ways to get the same result).

Among them is the greatest secret in alchemy. It’s called the “invention of sulfur water” and is the recipe at the start of this chapter. Sulfur and lime (calcium oxide, not the fruit) are gardening supplies that you can buy in a hardware store, and if you don’t have a small child that needs a wee to hand, strong vinegar from the supermarket will work just as well. While you shouldn’t try this at home, the result, after you heat the mix for an hour, is a red-brown goop and a kitchen that reeks of rotten eggs. These are calcium polysulfides, making up lime sulfur. It’s a nasty substance – an alkali that can cause skin irritation and even blindness if you get it in your eyes. Today, we use this for pest control, but in ancient times it was how you created gold. Well, the appearance of gold. Once you’ve got your “sulfur water”, any metal object submersed – a coin, nail or paperclip – will gain a thin, yellowy film coating.

The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t just the oldest alchemy book in history. It’s a tried-and-tested guide for tricksters. We may not know who wrote the document, but we do know that if you had walked into the author’s workshop 1,700 years ago, you’d have been swindled. Or that’s how it seems. The truth, as we’ll learn, is that something else was going on that’s even more fascinating. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

The 28 best popular science books of 2026

From space-time to saunas, here are the very best popular science books published this year that you should be adding to your Christmas list

The Leiden Papyrus X isn’t what most people think of when they picture alchemy. We think of it as a pseudoscience, a blend of religious beliefs, ancient superstition and gilded dreams, with only the occasional glimpse of something that might work underneath. If you subscribe to the traditional view, this is the best you can hope for when it comes to studying any chemistry earlier than about 1650. Before the Enlightenment, there were only wizards, witches and wishful thinking. Then suddenly, whoosh, in a flash of gunpowder, a crackle of electricity and bubbling fizz from a test tube, a new science arrived to change our world.

This book turns that idea on its head. No one person created chemistry, and even if they had, it certainly wouldn’t have been some white European in a powdered wig. Chemistry didn’t appear overnight and there is no one moment when it came into existence. It was a gradual transformation that built on millennia of knowledge. Choosing to ignore chemistry during the Age of Alchemy does a disservice to thousands of men and women, across the world, who guided us from the first campfire to the modern age.

This book is divided into three parts. In the first, we look at how early chemistry worked, from the Stone Age up to the emergence of alchemy, and how it set the basic principles for what alchemy, and later chemistry, would become. In the second, we go on a trip around the world. Practically every history of alchemy just focuses on the western traditions – mainly because they are the best studied. But we’re going to look at what was happening with chemistry in the Islamic world, China, the Indian subcontinent and even the Americas. Some of this is alchemy, and some of it isn’t, but it all plays a role in the tapestry of science. Finally, the third section returns to Europe, where we’ll look at how alchemy changed (or, to use the alchemical term, transmuted), over the course of several hundred years, into the science we know today. My journey has led to travels across six continents and taken me on adventures through deserts and jungles, tombs and tomes, and some of our most fabled cities. I have explored old roads and met the researchers busy paving new ones. The result is a story that is both a mirror to progress and a love letter to science, one that offers a glimpse into the past and shows how it all connects to our daily lives, often in surprising and roundabout ways. Chemistry is everywhere and is linked to everything. It is painfully human. It is filled with our mistakes, beliefs and hubris. It showcases our noble endeavours, destructive potential and indomitable spirit. And it allows us to appreciate how science, whether through petty rivalries, oppression and colonisation, or religious fervour, has always been political.

© Kit Chapman

This is an extract from The Age of Alchemy by Kit Chapman, the December read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.
